title: A Windy Day Mystery
text: It was a very windy day in the garden. Abdul saw that a small pea plant's stick support broke and it fell over. But the huge neem tree nearby didn't even move! This is our first mystery.

title: Think Like a Scientist
text: Why do you think the big heavy tree didn't fall down in the strong wind, but the small plant did? What could be holding the tree so firmly to the ground?

content.title: The Hidden Grip
content.description: Just like your fingers gripping a ball tightly, a tree has a hidden network under the soil holding it tight.

title: The Secret Underground Helpers
text: The hidden parts of the plant under the soil are called Roots. They act like an anchor, gripping the soil tightly to keep the plant standing straight.

content.definition: The part of a plant that grows underground, holds it in place, and takes in water and nutrients from the soil.

question: What is the main function of the roots in keeping a tree upright?
options: They make food for the tree.
They hold the tree firmly in the soil.
They give shade to the soil.

content.title: Reflection: The Grass Pull
content.text: Imagine trying to pull out a small patch of grass from the ground. It is surprisingly hard! That's because even small grass has many tiny roots holding the soil.

title: Connecting to the Real World
text: Just like a ship uses a heavy metal anchor to stay in one place in the moving ocean, a tree uses its roots as an anchor to stay in place during storms.

content.title: Mastery Task
content.text: Next time you go to a garden, gently pull a small weed (with an adult's permission) and observe its roots. See how much soil comes up with it!

title: The Thirsty Plant Mystery
text: Abdul noticed that if he only sprayed water on the leaves of a plant, it still started to dry up. But when he poured water on the soil, the plant became fresh again.

title: Socratic Question
text: If the leaves need water, how does the water from the soil travel all the way up to the top of the plant?

content.title: Nature's Straws
content.description: Roots act like tiny straws, sucking up water from the soil and sending it up the stem to the leaves.

title: Roots that we eat!
text: Roots don't just absorb water. Some plants store their extra food in their roots. When we eat carrots, radishes, or beetroots, we are actually eating roots!

content.definition: A large, main root that grows straight down, like a carrot or radish.

question: Which of the following vegetables is actually a root?

content.title: Kitchen Exploration
content.text: Ask students to look in their kitchen and classify vegetables into roots, stems, and leaves.

title: Connection: Storing for Later
text: Just like we store extra food in a refrigerator to eat later, the plant stores extra food in its roots.

content.title: Potatoes are NOT Roots!
content.text: Even though potatoes grow underground, they are actually modified stems, not roots. True roots don't have 'eyes' (buds) like potatoes do.

title: The Hanging Ropes Mystery
text: Abdul went to a park and saw a massive Banyan tree. He saw children swinging on thick rope-like things hanging from the branches.

title: Socratic Question
text: Are these hanging ropes just special branches, or could they be something else trying to reach the ground?

content.title: Roots from the Sky
content.description: These are special roots that grow down from the branches. When they reach the ground, they go inside and act like strong pillars.

title: Aerial Roots (Prop Roots)
text: The hanging ropes of the Banyan tree are called aerial roots or prop roots. Because the Banyan tree has very heavy branches, it needs extra support. These roots grow into the soil and become like pillars.

content.definition: Roots that grow above the ground, often from stems or branches, to support the plant.

question: Why does a Banyan tree have roots hanging from its branches?
options: To provide extra support like pillars for its heavy branches.
To make the tree look beautiful.

content.title: Reflection: Pillars of Strength
content.text: Think about a large building. Can a huge roof be supported by just one central wall? No, it needs pillars. The Banyan tree uses prop roots as its pillars.

title: Connecting to Architecture
text: Ancient Indian architecture used pillars in massive temples, much like how the ancient Banyan tree uses prop roots to support its sprawling canopy.

content.title: Mastery Challenge
content.text: Draw a huge Banyan tree. Make sure to add the prop roots hanging from the branches and entering the ground like strong pillars.
